title: Gallstone Disease: Conservative Management versus Elective Cholecystectomy

evidenceAudit.scope: Adult with gallstones found on ultrasound who has had biliary colic or one episode of uncomplicated symptoms, seen in a Saudi clinic: confirm the diagnosis, exclude complications, explain the choice between watchful conservative management and elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy, give pain relief, consider bile acid dissolution in selected patients, and set the return plan. Not for acute cholecystitis, cholangitis, gallstone pancreatitis or obstructive jaundice, which need urgent hospital care. Uses the C-GALL randomised trial, a Saudi patient survey and the product labels.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-14.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi or Gulf national guideline on elective management of symptomatic gallstones was found. The main evidence is the United Kingdom C-GALL randomised trial (434 adults) and its health technology assessment report; its health-service setting and surgical waiting times differ from Saudi hospitals.

The European (EASL 2016), Tokyo and World Society of Emergency Surgery guidelines could not be opened from this environment, so no recommendation grades from them are given; the topic does not state how guidelines advise on asymptomatic stones or on timing of cholecystectomy after acute cholecystitis.
The C-GALL trial follow-up is 18 to 24 months; longer-term outcomes, and which patients do best with surgery, are not established, and the report says some scenarios reversed the cost findings.

Saudi data used: a cross-sectional survey of 886 Saudi patients after laparoscopic cholecystectomy (61.6% satisfied, 25.4% very satisfied, 39.5% reported complications or adverse effects); it is self-reported, has no conservative comparison group, and does not give national prevalence.

Prevalence of gallstones in Saudi Arabia, and risk groups such as sickle cell disease, rapid weight loss and bariatric surgery, were not verified from a source read here and are not stated as numbers.

Ursodiol: the label is a United States label that limits use to radiolucent, noncalcified stones under 20 mm in patients who decline or cannot have surgery; Saudi registration and local brand availability were not checked.
Pregnancy, breastfeeding and renal-dose information for ursodiol were not found in the label text read; check a reference before use in those groups.

Ibuprofen and acetaminophen labels are over-the-counter drug facts labels for short self-treatment; the doses written are label doses and a clinician may prescribe within the prescription label. Ketorolac is written from the United States label for hospital use only.
Antispasmodics (for example hyoscine butylbromide) and opioid doses for severe colic were not reviewed, so no regimen is written for them.
Figures were read by automated extraction of web and label text; spot-check each figure and dose against the source during clinical review.

pathophysiology.summary: Stones in the gallbladder can block the cystic duct and cause pain called biliary colic; most people with uncomplicated symptomatic stones do not develop complications, with reported complication rates as low as 1 to 3% a year (C-GALL trial (BMJ 2023), Section Introduction). Complications are acute cholecystitis, pancreatitis, cholangitis and obstructive jaundice (C-GALL trial (BMJ 2023), Section Introduction). Gallstones are common: prevalence of 6% to 25% is described worldwide and rises with age (C-GALL trial (BMJ 2023), Section Introduction). Cholecystectomy removes the organ but is not free of harm: 10.8% had complications within 30 days in a large United Kingdom study, and about 20% have persistent pain like the pain before surgery (C-GALL trial (BMJ 2023), Section Introduction). Ursodiol changes bile from cholesterol-precipitating to cholesterol-solubilising and can dissolve only radiolucent cholesterol stones (Ursodiol label, Section Clinical Pharmacology).

symptoms: Episodic right upper abdominal pain (biliary colic) or acute cholecystitis in the past (C-GALL trial (BMJ 2023), Section Methods, Participants).
Pain linked to gallstones seen on imaging in a person referred for elective care (C-GALL trial (BMJ 2023), Section Methods, Participants).
Persistent symptoms may continue after surgery in some patients, so clarify what the pain is (C-GALL trial (BMJ 2023), Section Introduction).
physicalSigns: Right upper abdominal tenderness during pain; examination may be normal between attacks (C-GALL trial (BMJ 2023), Section Methods, Participants).
Jaundice, fever or marked tenderness suggest a complication and need urgent assessment (C-GALL trial (BMJ 2023), Section Results, Complications).
redFlags: Fever with right upper abdominal pain and tenderness, suggesting acute cholecystitis (C-GALL trial (BMJ 2023), Section Results, Complications).
Jaundice, dark urine or pale stools, with or without fever: biliary obstruction or cholangitis (Ursodiol label, Section Contraindications).
Severe upper abdominal pain radiating to the back with vomiting: gallstone pancreatitis (C-GALL trial (BMJ 2023), Section Results, Complications).
Pain not settling with simple analgesia, or repeated attacks: refer for surgical assessment (C-GALL trial (BMJ 2023), Section Discussion).
Stones with a gallbladder polyp or wall change on ultrasound: refer to a surgeon (Ursodiol label, Section Indications and Usage).
precipitants: Rapid weight loss: ursodiol is labelled to prevent stone formation in obese patients losing weight rapidly (Ursodiol label, Section Indications and Usage).
Fatty meals can bring on an attack in some people, but this was not tested in the sources read (C-GALL trial (BMJ 2023), Section Methods).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Episodic right upper abdominal pain with stones on ultrasound and no fever or jaundice (C-GALL trial (BMJ 2023), Section Methods, Participants).
Constant pain with tenderness and fever, raised inflammatory markers and thickened gallbladder wall (C-GALL trial (BMJ 2023), Section Methods, Participants).
Jaundice, deranged liver tests or raised lipase (Ursodiol label, Section Contraindications).
Burning epigastric pain related to meals, no stones; stones may be incidental (Ketorolac label, Section Contraindications for ulcer risk with NSAIDs).
About 20% have pain like the pain before surgery, so confirm the pain is biliary before surgery (C-GALL trial (BMJ 2023), Section Introduction).

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm gallstones as the cause of the pain
actions: Take a history of episodic right upper abdominal pain and past episodes of cholecystitis; examine the abdomen (C-GALL trial (BMJ 2023), Section Methods, Participants).
Confirm stones with ultrasound before offering the choice between surgery and observation (C-GALL trial (BMJ 2023), Section Methods, Participants).
If the pain is not typical, consider other causes, because about 20% of patients keep pain after cholecystectomy (C-GALL trial (BMJ 2023), Section Introduction).

clinicalManagement.title: Exclude complications
actions: Check temperature and look for jaundice; send liver profile, lipase, full blood count and C-reactive protein (Ursodiol label, Section Contraindications).
If cholecystitis, cholangitis, obstruction or pancreatitis is suspected, arrange urgent hospital care (Ursodiol label, Section Contraindications).

clinicalManagement.title: Discuss the choice: observe or operate
actions: Explain that by 18 months pain scores were equal with conservative management and with surgery (C-GALL trial (BMJ 2023), Section Results).
Explain that 25% of people in the conservative arm still had surgery by 18 months and 67% in the surgery arm (C-GALL trial (BMJ 2023), Section Results).

Explain that gallstone-specific quality of life at 24 months favoured surgery, while complication rates did not differ significantly (C-GALL HTA report 2024, Results; C-GALL trial (BMJ 2023), Section Results, Complications).
Explain the risks of surgery: 10.8% had complications within 30 days in a United Kingdom cohort, and about 20% have persistent pain after (C-GALL trial (BMJ 2023), Section Introduction).

Share the Saudi experience: most patients were satisfied after laparoscopic cholecystectomy, but 39.5% reported a complication or adverse effect (Saudi laparoscopic cholecystectomy survey, Section Results).
Record the patient's decision and values; either route is reasonable for uncomplicated disease (C-GALL trial (BMJ 2023), Section Discussion).

clinicalManagement.title: Treat attacks of pain
actions: Give an oral anti-inflammatory tablet for pain unless it is unsuitable, or paracetamol (acetaminophen) (Ibuprofen label, Section Directions; Acetaminophen label, Section Directions).

For severe pain in a hospital setting a single dose of injectable ketorolac can be used for no more than 5 days, after checking kidney function and ulcer history (Ketorolac label, Section Dosage and Administration).
Advise on the red flags and give a plan to attend if pain lasts more than a few hours or fever or jaundice appears (C-GALL trial (BMJ 2023), Section Results, Complications).

clinicalManagement.title: Carry out the plan chosen
actions: If surgery: refer for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy (C-GALL trial (BMJ 2023), Section Methods, Interventions).
If observation: give written advice and review for new attacks or complications; the median time to later surgery was 9.0 months in the conservative group (C-GALL HTA report 2024, Results).
If stones are radiolucent, noncalcified and under 20 mm and surgery is declined or unsafe, consider ursodiol (Ursodiol label, Section Indications and Usage).

clinicalManagement.title: Review
actions: Review the patient at the interval agreed; reassess if attacks recur, because the trial shows people moved to surgery during follow-up (C-GALL trial (BMJ 2023), Section Results).

If ursodiol is used, repeat ultrasound every 6 months in the first year and stop if the gallbladder stops visualising or no dissolution is seen at 12 months (Ursodiol label, Section Dosage and Administration).

regimens.indication: Short-term relief of biliary colic pain
regimens.patientGroup: Adults with biliary colic who can take an oral anti-inflammatory tablet
regimens.dose: 200 mg to 400 mg every 4 to 6 hours as needed, with no more than 1,200 mg in 24 hours unless a doctor directs (Ibuprofen label, Directions). Dilution and preparation: none; oral tablet.
regimens.route: Oral with water; take with food or milk if the stomach is upset (Ibuprofen label, Directions)
regimens.duration: Shortest time possible; ask a doctor if pain lasts more than 10 days (Ibuprofen label, Stop use)
adjustments: Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time (Ibuprofen label, Directions).
Pregnant or breast-feeding women should ask a health professional before use (Ibuprofen label, Pregnancy or breast-feeding).
Kidney disease, heart disease, high blood pressure, cirrhosis or a diuretic: ask a doctor first (Ibuprofen label, Ask a doctor before use).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Stomach pain, black stools or vomiting blood: stop and seek care (Ibuprofen label, Stop use).
Pain with fever or jaundice: stop and assess for complication (C-GALL trial (BMJ 2023), Section Results, Complications).
contraindications: Previous allergic reaction to ibuprofen or other pain relievers, including aspirin-triggered asthma (Ibuprofen label, Do not use).
Right before or after heart surgery (Ibuprofen label, Do not use).
Ask a doctor first with stomach ulcer or bleeding (Ibuprofen label, Ask a doctor before use).
regimens.useWhen: First choice for an attack of colic when no stomach, kidney, asthma or heart problem prevents an anti-inflammatory.

regimens.indication: Short-term relief of severe biliary colic pain in hospital
regimens.patientGroup: Adults in hospital with severe colic, no ulcer, bleeding risk, asthma or kidney problem
regimens.dose: Single dose: 30 mg intravenously or 60 mg intramuscularly for age under 65; 15 mg intravenously or 30 mg intramuscularly for age 65 or over, weight under 50 kg or kidney impairment (Ketorolac label, Dosage and Administration). Multiple doses: 30 mg every 6 hours, maximum 120 mg a day; 15 mg every 6 hours, maximum 60 mg a day for age 65 or over, kidney impairment or weight under 50 kg. Dilution and preparation: no dilution is described; use the vial strength (15 mg per mL, 30 mg per mL or 60 mg per 2 mL); do not mix in a small syringe with morphine, meperidine, promethazine or hydroxyzine because ketorolac precipitates (Ketorolac label, Pharmaceutical Information).
regimens.route: Intravenous bolus over no less than 15 seconds, or slow deep intramuscular injection; the 60 mg per 2 mL vial is for intramuscular use only; never neuraxial (Ketorolac label, Dosage and Administration and Contraindications)
regimens.frequency: Single dose or every 6 hours as needed; analgesia begins in about 30 minutes and lasts 4 to 6 hours
regimens.duration: Not more than 5 days in total, including any oral ketorolac (Ketorolac label, Dosage and Administration)
adjustments: Correct low blood volume before giving (Ketorolac label, Dosage and Administration).
Age 65 or over, weight under 50 kg or kidney impairment: use the lower dose and a maximum of 60 mg a day (Ketorolac label, Dosage and Administration).
Not indicated for children (Ketorolac label, Warnings).
Contraindicated in labor and delivery; avoid in pregnancy beyond what the label allows (Ketorolac label, Contraindications).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Stomach bleeding, ulcer or perforation signs (Ketorolac label, Warnings, Gastrointestinal).
Kidney function and urine output (Ketorolac label, Warnings, Renal Effects).
Bleeding, especially with anticoagulants (Ketorolac label, Warnings, Hemorrhage).
Anaphylactoid reaction and asthma (Ketorolac label, Warnings, Anaphylactoid Reactions).
contraindications: Active peptic ulcer, recent or past gastrointestinal bleeding or perforation (Ketorolac label, Contraindications).
Aspirin or NSAID-triggered asthma, urticaria or allergy (Ketorolac label, Contraindications).
Advanced renal impairment or volume depletion; cerebrovascular bleeding, bleeding disorder or high bleeding risk (Ketorolac label, Contraindications).
Current aspirin or other NSAID use; probenecid; pentoxifylline; coronary bypass surgery; labor and delivery (Ketorolac label, Contraindications).
regimens.useWhen: Choose only in hospital for moderately severe colic that other pain relievers do not control.

regimens.indication: Dissolution of radiolucent noncalcified gallbladder stones under 20 mm in patients for whom elective surgery would be done except for risk, or who refuse surgery
regimens.patientGroup: Adults with radiolucent noncalcified gallbladder stones under 20 mm and increased surgical risk or refusal of surgery
regimens.dose: 8 mg to 10 mg per kg per day in 2 or 3 divided doses (Ursodiol label, Dosage and Administration); calculate from actual body weight and round to whole 300 mg capsules. Prevention of stones during rapid weight loss: 600 mg a day as 300 mg twice a day (Ursodiol label, Dosage and Administration). Dilution and preparation: none; supplied as 300 mg capsules (Ursodiol label, Description).
regimens.frequency: Two or three times a day
regimens.duration: Months of treatment; safety beyond 24 months is not established; stop if no partial dissolution by 12 months or if the gallbladder stops visualising (Ursodiol label, Indications and Usage and Dosage and Administration)
adjustments: Complete dissolution is expected in about 30% of unselected patients with uncalcified stones under 20 mm treated for up to 2 years; 81% with stones up to 5 mm (Ursodiol label, Clinical Studies).
Stones recur in up to 50% of patients within 5 years of dissolution (Ursodiol label, Clinical Studies).
Doses of 16 to 20 mg per kg a day were tolerated by 7 patients; overdose is most likely to cause diarrhoea (Ursodiol label, Overdosage).
No more than caution in the elderly (Ursodiol label, Geriatric Use).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Ultrasound every 6 months in the first year; confirm dissolution by ultrasound 1 to 3 months after it first appears (Ursodiol label, Dosage and Administration).
Alanine and aspartate aminotransferase at the start and as indicated (Ursodiol label, Precautions, Liver Tests).
Obstructive bowel symptoms in people with intestinal stenosis or stasis: hold the drug and evaluate (Ursodiol label, Warnings).
contraindications: Calcified cholesterol stones, radiopaque stones or radiolucent pigment stones (Ursodiol label, Contraindications).
Compelling reasons for surgery: unremitting acute cholecystitis, cholangitis, biliary obstruction, gallstone pancreatitis or biliary-gastrointestinal fistula (Ursodiol label, Contraindications).
Allergy to bile acids (Ursodiol label, Contraindications).

teaching.scope: Adult with gallstones found on ultrasound who has had biliary colic or one episode of uncomplicated symptoms, seen in a Saudi clinic: confirm the diagnosis, exclude complications, explain the choice between watchful conservative management and elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy, give pain relief, consider bile acid dissolution in selected patients, and set the return plan. Not for acute cholecystitis, cholangitis, gallstone pancreatitis or obstructive jaundice, which need urgent hospital care. Uses the C-GALL randomised trial, a Saudi patient survey and the product labels.
learningObjectives: Confirm stones on ultrasound and exclude complications before offering the choice.
For uncomplicated symptomatic stones, observation and surgery gave equal pain scores at 18 months.
Surgery helps gallstone-specific quality of life more at 24 months; observation costs less and avoids surgical complications.
Treat attacks with an anti-inflammatory or paracetamol and teach the red flags.
pitfalls: Operating on pain that is not biliary.
Offering observation without a plan for red flags.
Giving ursodiol for calcified stones or when surgery is needed.
Using ketorolac with another NSAID or in kidney impairment.
keyPoints: Fever, jaundice or pain radiating to the back mean urgent hospital care.
Ursodiol only works on radiolucent noncalcified stones under 20 mm and stones recur in up to half within 5 years.
Ketorolac must not exceed 5 days and has many contraindications.

patientEducation: Most people with gallstones do not get serious problems, but attacks of pain can recur.
You can choose surgery or watchful waiting; both gave the same pain scores at 18 months in a large trial.
About 1 in 4 people who chose watchful waiting still had surgery within 18 months.
Go to the hospital if you have fever, yellow eyes or skin, dark urine, or severe pain that does not settle.
Take pain tablets with food and do not combine different anti-inflammatory tablets.
lifestyleAndDiet: Keep a symptom diary to see if attacks follow fatty meals.

Keep a healthy weight and stay active.

mdtReferrals: Primary care physician or surgeon; radiologist for ultrasound; nurse educator; pharmacist; gastroenterologist for bile duct stones or ursodiol; anaesthetist before surgery.
dischargeCriteria: Decision between observation and surgery documented; red flags and the hospital attendance plan given; pain reliever prescribed; surgical referral sent or review date booked.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review at the agreed interval (for example 3 to 6 months) or sooner for new attacks; if ursodiol is used, ultrasound every 6 months in the first year.
